intro: The second movement of Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5, Op. 67, marked Andante con moto, opens with violas and cellos playing a theme in A♭ major over pizzicato basses. Beethoven varies the theme repeatedly, and trumpets and timpani break in several times with a fanfare in C major.

sections.label: A · A♭ major theme, C major fanfare
sections.mNote: An A♭ major melody in low strings, then a C major fanfare.

sections.label: A′ · Melody varied in semiquavers
sections.mNote: Violas and cellos play the opening melody in semiquaver figuration.

sections.label: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
sections.mNote: Demisemiquavers in the low strings; clarinet, bassoon and flute follow.

sections.label: B · Fanfare theme turns to minor
sections.mNote: Quieter string figures lead towards A♭ minor.

sections.label: A‴ · Tune in full orchestra
sections.mNote: A♭ major returns over fast figures in the lower strings.

sections.label: Coda · Bassoon, Più moto
sections.mNote: Più moto, then Tempo I and the final A♭.

cues.title: Opening theme, violas and cellos
cues.text: The violins rest. Violas and cellos play the A♭ major melody in octaves, in a dotted rhythm, while the double basses play pizzicato beneath. Beethoven marks the tune dolce, sweetly.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Werke, Serie 1 No. 5, Breitkopf & Härtel, printed p. 22, opening of Andante con moto: viola and cello octaves, pizzicato bass and dolce. Mutopia 1437 reproduces these parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dotted tune in C major, tutti
cues.text: The orchestra moves into C major. Trumpets and timpani reinforce the dotted tune, and the strings run beneath it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, printed p. 23: C-major statement with trumpets, timpani and running string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First variation, violas and cellos
cues.text: Violas and cellos play the opening melody again in A♭ major, now filling its outline with semiquavers. The basses support them pizzicato, as before. The metre remains 3/8.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 24, first variation; Mutopia 1437, viola, cello and bass parts. The metre remains 3/8.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Lobkowitz and Razumovsky
cues.text: The Fifth is dedicated jointly to Prince Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky. Both names also appear on the Sixth Symphony, which was first performed with it in 1808.
cues.evidence: Dedication and joint première of the Fifth and Sixth: Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/.

cues.title: Choral Fantasy, 22 December 1808
cues.text: The Choral Fantasy, which ended the concert of 22 December 1808, went wrong. Beethoven forgot the plan he had given the players and repeated a section, so the concertmaster stopped and called out dryly, “Again!” Afterwards Beethoven asked the orchestra’s pardon.
cues.evidence: Ignaz von Seyfried, appendix to Beethoven’s Studien (1832), p. 15, as translated in Thayer, The Life of Ludwig van Beethoven, ed. Krehbiel (1921), vol. 2, pp. 130–131: https://archive.org/details/lifeofludwigvanb02thay

cues.title: Variation in demisemiquavers
cues.text: The lower strings divide the tune into demisemiquavers, quicker than the earlier semiquavers. The outline of the melody is still there in the fast bow strokes. After a fermata, clarinet, bassoon and flute play a quieter succession of phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 27–30: demisemiquaver variation, fermata and woodwind continuation. Mutopia 1437, cello part, distinguishes this return from the earlier semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition, 1804–1808
cues.text: Beethoven sketched the Fifth in 1804, soon after the Eroica, and finished it in 1808. In the intervening years he wrote Fidelio, the Razumovsky quartets, the Appassionata, the Violin Concerto, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Fourth Symphony.
cues.evidence: Composition history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven), History: Composition; dates 1804–05 and 1807–08 at the Eastman School of Music, https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: Third fanfare and A♭ minor episode
cues.text: The third fanfare in C major dies away. Trumpets and timpani drop out, leaving smaller figures in the strings and woodwind. The tune moves into A♭ minor before the opening melody returns in full in A♭ major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 31–33: diminuendo, reduced scoring, A♭-minor passage and following A♭-major return. The cue covers the episode beginning at the existing section boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme, A♭ major
cues.text: The opening tune returns in A♭ major, fortissimo. The line that began in violas and cellos now goes to the winds and violins, and the lower strings play quick accompanying figures.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 33, lower system: full A♭-major return, ff, melody in winds and first violins, rapid lower-string accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, bassoon solo
cues.text: In the coda, marked Più moto, the bassoon has a short solo above detached strings, still in 3/8 and in A♭. Tempo I later restores the opening pace for the last phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 34–35: Più moto, bassoon solo and detached strings, followed by Tempo I.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Esterházy payment, December 1808
cues.text: What the concert of 22 December 1808 earned for Beethoven is not known. A record shows that Prince Nikolaus Esterházy, who had commissioned the Mass in C, ordered 100 gulden paid to him for the benefit.
cues.evidence: Thayer, The Life of Ludwig van Beethoven, rev. Elliot Forbes (Princeton, 1964): the “pecuniary results” of the concert of 22 December 1808 “are not known”, but a record has Prince Esterházy ordering 100 gulden paid to Beethoven, citing the Grenzboten of 13 November 1868 (TDR III, 84 n. 1).

cues.title: Final cadences in A♭ major
cues.text: In the final cadences the bass moves from E♭ to A♭. The movement ends in A♭ major, the key of the opening theme in the low strings, with the full orchestra playing.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 36: closing E♭–A♭ cadences and orchestral A♭-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bass descent back to A♭ major
transitions.from: A · A♭ major theme, C major fanfare
transitions.how: After the C major fanfare, the bass descends E–E♭–D–D♭–C, then moves through D♭ to E♭, the dominant of A♭ major. Violas and cellos play the opening melody again in semiquavers, above plucked basses. The brass rests. The Andante tempo is unchanged.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 23–24; Mutopia 1437, cello and bass parts, chromatic link and first variation.

transitions.title: Second chromatic descent to A♭ major
transitions.to: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
transitions.how: The C major fanfare again ends as the bass descends E–E♭–D–D♭–C. The harmony returns to A♭ major, and the low strings play the melody in demisemiquavers. The bars stay in 3/8, so more notes fall within each bar, and the varied line keeps the rise and fall of the original tune.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 27–28; Mutopia 1437, cello part, second chromatic link and demisemiquaver return.

transitions.title: Trumpets and timpani stop
transitions.from: A″ · Quicker notes, then woodwind solos
transitions.to: B · Fanfare theme turns to minor
transitions.how: The C major fanfare makes a diminuendo. Trumpets and timpani stop. The strings carry on with short repeated figures, which pass between the upper and lower parts, and the woodwind then enter. In the A♭ minor passage that follows, C♭ and G♭ are added to the outline of the theme.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 31–32, diminuendo and subsequent minor-mode writing; Mutopia 1437 cello part includes C♭ and G♭.

transitions.title: Fortissimo return of the opening melody
transitions.from: B · Fanfare theme turns to minor
transitions.how: Rising figures pass through the strings, and a crescendo brings in the winds. The opening melody returns fortissimo in A♭ major. Winds and first violins play it together, while violas and cellos accompany in quick notes above an A♭ in the basses.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 33, crescendo and full A♭-major return.

transitions.title: The bassoon solo at Più moto
transitions.how: The full A♭ major statement is followed by quieter strings. At Più moto, a bassoon plays a solo above detached string chords and short bass notes, and the bar of three quavers is kept. The wind and strings build another crescendo by degrees, and Tempo I then restores the original pace.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 34–35: Più moto bassoon solo, detached strings, crescendo and Tempo I.

source.title: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, II, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate B.5
source.locator: Printed pp. 22–36; viola, cello and bass parts also in Mutopia 1437.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos play the dotted melody above pizzicato double basses.
The wind instruments follow the low strings, and the violins then enter.
Trumpets and timpani join the C-major fanfare, with running strings beneath it.
The brass stops while the bass descends by semitones.
Violas and cellos decorate the melody in semiquavers beneath a held clarinet note and plucked violins.
Clarinets and bassoons answer the strings’ decorated melody.
Trumpets and timpani return for the second C-major fanfare.
The bass repeats its chromatic descent as the trumpets and timpani stop.
Violas and cellos play demisemiquavers under held wind notes and plucked violins.
Quick lower-string figures run beneath accented orchestral chords.
After a fermata, clarinet, bassoon and flute play phrases over detached strings.
The full orchestra plays the third C-major fanfare.
Small string figures and woodwind replies lead towards A♭ minor.
Winds and violins play the opening tune fortissimo above quick lower strings.
A bassoon plays a melody above detached strings at Più moto.
Tempo I restores the opening pace, with wind replies above the strings.
The orchestra plays a crescendo into the final cadences in A♭ major.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
